problem: Topological-map ImageNav methods (e.g. VGM) feed all node features to the policy, so they are misled by goal-irrelevant nodes, and each node only holds a local view, so there is no scene-level representation.
motivation: Multi-goal navigation needs the agent to revisit explored places and plan efficient routes. Pilot visualizations of goal-decoder attention show that high scores fall on nodes leading to the goal and little attention goes to remote ones. This suggests that using only the goal-relevant part of memory, plus a global summary, should be more efficient.
key_idea: A working-memory-inspired pipeline: forget low-attention map nodes (STM), add a global node aggregating the map (LTM), and encode both with GATv2 into a working memory (WM) that the policy decodes.
insight: Attention-based forgetting and a learned global node are complementary. In the component ablation, forget alone or LTM alone gives modest gains, forget+LTM gives more, and adding GATv2 (WM) is best (1-goal SR 52.1 -> 62.4 over VGM on the full 1400 episodes). Replacing the LTM with a random STM feature or an averaged STM hurts, so the learned adaptive aggregation matters. The best forgetting ratio depends on task horizon: lower p for 1-2 goals, higher p for longer tasks (4-goal peaks at p=0.4), because agents revisit explored areas and benefit from a small goal-relevant subset.
method: Topological map / STM: inherits VGM's map and localization; node features from a pretrained RGB-D panoramic encoder are the short-term memory, with a 100-node queue.

Selective forgetting: after D_goal decodes, nodes whose goal-attention scores rank in the bottom p (=20%) are disconnected and excluded from later steps. They are restored if the agent revisits them or a goal is reached. The module is plug-and-play, switched off in training and on at evaluation.
LTM global node: a zero-initialized trainable global node connected to all map nodes, recurrent over time, which aggregates STM features and bridges sub-graphs split by forgotten nodes.
WM generation: GATv2 encodes {retained STM, LTM} with adaptive neighbor weights into the working memory M_w.
Action generation: two Transformer decoders D_cur (query = current embedding) and D_goal (query = goal embedding) decode M_w. An LSTM policy takes [f_cur, f_goal, e_cur] and outputs action logits.
Training: same pipeline as VGM: imitation learning (1.5 days) then PPO fine-tuning (5 days) on Gibson 1-goal data, with VGM's reward and auxiliary losses.

setting.backbone: VGM-style pretrained RGB-D encoder + GATv2 + 2 Transformer decoders + LSTM policy (trained; imitation learning then PPO)
setting.training_data: Gibson 1-goal ImageNav dataset, 72 training scenes; no extra data
setting.observation: RGB-D panoramic (main); goal RGB image; no GPS/IMU. Also a 90°-FoV non-panoramic variant.

results: MemoNav beats VGM on Gibson in SR/PR at all levels: 1-goal SR 74.7 vs 70.0, 2-goal PR 50.8 vs 42.9, 3-goal 38.0 vs 29.5, 4-goal 28.9 vs 21.5. On Matterport3D it gets consistently higher SR/PR than VGM and TSGM, but not SPL or PPL: VGM is slightly better on 1-goal SPL and TSGM on some PPL. With a 90° FoV camera it reaches 65.6 SR on Split A (vs OVRL+ZER-Reward 54.2) and 58.5 on Split B (vs SLING 54.8), though SLING has higher SPL (37.3).
limitations: Forgetting is a post-processing step using decoder attention, is not trained, and uses a fixed threshold p; it also does not reduce memory footprint because forgotten nodes stay in the map for localization.

Trained only on Gibson (western-style scenes) and evaluated only in simulation; generalization to Matterport3D is much lower (SR ~26), and failure modes remain (stopping mistakenly, missing the goal, over-exploring).
